inputs.need:
I lead the perioperative value programme for a regional health authority with eight hospitals. Surgeons and anaesthetists still order routine preoperative tests for healthy adults having low-risk ambulatory surgery: electrocardiograms, chest radiographs, full blood counts and coagulation studies, although our regional guidance has said for three years that they are not needed. A snapshot of 1,200 cataract, hernia and arthroscopy patients last spring found that 61 percent had at least one test the guidance advises against. The executive committee has asked which strategies actually reduce this kind of low-value testing, and whether stopping tests leads to more cancellations on the day of surgery or to harm.

We want to do a rapid review of strategies for reducing low-value preoperative testing in adults having low-risk ambulatory or elective surgery: feedback to clinicians on their own ordering, changes to order sets and electronic defaults, triage in the pre-anaesthesia clinic, clinician education, and materials for patients. We need to know which strategies, alone or combined, reduced testing, by how much, how long the effect lasted, and whether same-day cancellations or perioperative complications changed. The committee meets in December, so we have ten weeks.

I need help with a focused question, the outcomes, a search and screening approach that is quick without being careless, and a way to report certainty that the committee will understand. A librarian and two analysts are available part time.

records.title: Feedback on individual ordering to reduce routine preoperative testing: a controlled before-after study in six hospitals
records.authors: Harrington-Oyelaran B, Mbeki-Lindholm S, Castro-Nakamura J
records.venue: Ashcombe Journal of Health Services Improvement
records.abstract: Three hospitals gave surgeons and anaesthetists quarterly feedback on their own rates of routine preoperative testing in low-risk ambulatory surgery, compared with peers, and three similar hospitals did not. Over 18 months, electrocardiogram ordering fell from 48 to 29 percent in feedback hospitals and from 47 to 44 percent in comparison hospitals. Chest radiograph ordering fell in both groups. Same-day cancellations did not change. The effect was largest for clinicians whose baseline rates were highest. Hospitals were not allocated at random, and one feedback hospital also changed its pre-anaesthesia clinic during the study.

records.title: Removing routine preoperative tests from electronic order sets: an interrupted time series
records.abstract: A regional health system removed chest radiographs and coagulation studies from the default preoperative order sets for low-risk ambulatory surgery, while leaving them available on request. Using 30 months of monthly data, we found an immediate fall in chest radiographs of 72 percent, sustained over 18 months after the change, and a 64 percent fall in coagulation studies. Tests ordered on request rose slightly. There was no change in same-day cancellations or in unplanned admissions within 30 days. The design cannot exclude other changes at the same time, but the size and timing of the fall make them an unlikely explanation.

records.title: Multicomponent strategies to reduce low-value preoperative tests: a systematic review
records.authors: Adeyemi-Pratt L, Holmberg-Ansah D, Tanaka-Oduya R, Fitzgerald-Silva M
records.abstract: We searched four databases for studies of strategies to reduce routine preoperative testing in low-risk surgery and included 26 studies, mostly before-after designs. Strategies that changed the ordering system, such as order set changes and electronic defaults, reduced testing more consistently than education or guidelines alone. Combinations of feedback and system changes produced the largest reductions. Only nine studies reported same-day cancellations and six reported perioperative complications, with no increase in either. Most studies were at high risk of bias, and effects beyond 12 months were rarely reported.

records.title: Same-day cancellations after reducing routine preoperative testing in ambulatory surgery
records.venue: Ashcombe Journal of Health Services Improvement
records.abstract: After a hospital stopped routine preoperative testing for healthy adults having ambulatory surgery, we compared same-day cancellations in the year before and the year after. Of 4,812 procedures before and 5,036 after, same-day cancellations were unchanged after routine tests were reduced (1.9 against 2.0 percent), and cancellations attributed to abnormal test results fell. Perioperative complications recorded in the surgical outcome register did not change. Surgeons initially expressed concern about cancellations, which fell away as the data were shared. The comparison is uncontrolled and covers one hospital.

records.title: Nurse triage in the pre-anaesthesia clinic and preoperative test ordering: an observational study
records.abstract: We compared test ordering for low-risk ambulatory surgery patients assessed by nurse-led triage in the pre-anaesthesia clinic with patients assessed by junior doctors in the same clinic. Patients triaged by nurses using a structured protocol received at least one routine test in 22 percent of cases, against 57 percent of patients assessed by junior doctors. Nurses were more likely to follow the protocol and to document why a test was ordered. Allocation to nurse or doctor depended on clinic staffing on the day, and case mix differed slightly. The study did not report cancellations or complications.

records.title: Why clinicians keep ordering low-value preoperative tests: an interview study with surgeons and anaesthetists
records.abstract: We interviewed 28 surgeons and anaesthetists in four hospitals about routine preoperative testing. Clinicians knew the guidance but continued ordering because of habit, fear of blame if a problem was missed, and the belief that colleagues expected results to be available. Many said that tests were ordered by default before any clinician saw the patient. Several said that seeing their own ordering compared with peers had changed their practice more than education. Clinicians proposed removing tests from default order sets and agreeing locally who is responsible for deciding when a test is needed.

records.title: Education alone and low-value preoperative test ordering: a comparison of hospitals
records.abstract: Four hospitals delivered an education programme on preoperative testing guidance to surgeons, anaesthetists and pre-anaesthesia clinic staff, and four comparable hospitals did not. Test ordering fell by about 10 percentage points in education hospitals in the first three months, but education alone produced no sustained reduction at twelve months, when ordering had returned to baseline. Comparison hospitals showed no change. Staff turnover meant that many clinicians at twelve months had not attended the education sessions. The authors conclude that education should be combined with changes to ordering systems.

records.title: What patients expect from preoperative testing: a survey of adults awaiting ambulatory surgery
records.abstract: We surveyed 640 adults awaiting ambulatory surgery about their expectations of preoperative testing; 71 percent responded. Most respondents expected blood tests before surgery and believed that tests made surgery safer, but 64 percent said they would be comfortable without tests if their surgeon or anaesthetist explained why they were not needed. Older respondents and those with previous surgery were more likely to expect tests. Few respondents knew that tests could lead to further investigations and delays. Patient-facing explanations may support reductions in testing, but the survey did not test any intervention.

response.synthesis: Eight retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. System changes such as removing tests from default order sets produced large and durable reductions, and feedback on clinicians' own ordering reduced testing beyond comparison hospitals. Nurse-led protocol triage was associated with less testing. Education alone faded within a year. Where reported, same-day cancellations and complications did not rise. Clinicians describe habit, fear of blame and default ordering as the drivers, and most patients would accept fewer tests if the reason were explained. The evidence supports a rapid review organised by strategy type, with cancellations and complications as balancing outcomes.
response.gradeRationale: One controlled before-after study and one interrupted time series with large, consistent effects for system and feedback strategies, supported by a review of mostly weaker studies; moderate certainty that system changes reduce testing, low certainty about balancing outcomes.
response.summary: Eight records appraised; five claims; overall certainty moderate for reduced testing.

response.overview: Rapid review, October to early December 2026, of strategies to reduce low-value preoperative testing in adults having low-risk ambulatory or elective surgery, organised by strategy type, with durability and balancing outcomes and certainty rated per outcome.
response.population: Studies of adults having low-risk ambulatory or elective surgery in which routine preoperative tests (electrocardiogram, chest radiograph, blood count, coagulation, biochemistry) are advised against by local or national guidance.
response.exposure: Any strategy to reduce low-value testing: ordering system changes (order sets, defaults, decision support), feedback on clinicians' own ordering, pre-anaesthesia clinic triage, clinician education, patient-facing materials, or combinations.
response.procedures: The librarian searches three databases and a trial register from 2010, in English, building on the 2021 review's strategy. One analyst screens titles and abstracts; the second screens a random 20 percent and all exclusions at full text. One analyst extracts with a piloted form and the second checks all outcome data. Studies are classified by strategy components. Risk of bias is assessed with design-appropriate short tools, and certainty is rated per outcome with GRADE.

response.designSummary: Narrative synthesis by strategy type with a structured summary table, an effect direction plot and GRADE certainty per outcome; meta-analysis only where comparable controlled studies allow it.
response.sampleSize: No sample size applies to a review. The expected yield is about 1,500 records and 30 to 40 included studies, based on the 2021 review's 26 studies plus later work. A random-effects meta-analysis is planned only when at least three controlled studies of the same strategy report the same outcome in comparable units; otherwise effects are reported study by study with their direction and size.
response.primaryAnalysis: For each strategy type, absolute change in the proportion of patients with at least one low-value test (or tests per patient) is tabulated with design, follow-up and risk of bias, and summarised in an effect direction plot; certainty is rated per strategy and outcome.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Durability at 12 months or later; single versus combined strategies described side by side; same-day cancellations and 30-day complications tabulated wherever reported, with the number of studies that did not report them.
response.missingData: Outcomes not reported are recorded as not reported, never assumed unchanged; study authors are not contacted within the ten-week window, which is stated as a limitation.
response.multiplicity: No hypothesis testing across strategies; comparisons between strategies are descriptive and labelled as indirect.
response.software: Reference manager for screening, a shared spreadsheet for extraction, and R for any meta-analysis and the effect direction plot.
overfittingGuards: No ranking of strategies from indirect comparisons presented as a finding
response.summary: Narrative synthesis by strategy with an effect direction plot; meta-analysis only with at least three comparable controlled studies.

response.risks: No participant risk; the risk is a policy decision resting on weak or incomplete evidence, especially for balancing outcomes.
response.data: Extraction forms and the summary table are kept on the programme's shared drive and appended to the committee paper.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: older patients and patients with previous surgery are more likely to expect tests, and patients with limited English may receive less explanation; any subgroup findings and patient-facing strategies are extracted, and the committee paper notes where evidence on these groups is absent.
response.effectiveness: The review succeeds if the committee can choose strategies with a clear view of expected size, durability and balancing effects.
response.efficiency: Rapid methods fit the ten-week window and part-time staff.
response.costs: Staff time within existing roles; library subscriptions only.
response.partnerships: The regional anaesthesia and surgery leads, pre-anaesthesia clinic nurses, the laboratory and imaging leads, and two patient partners from the regional patient council.
response.rebPath: No research ethics review is needed for a review of published literature; the protocol will be posted on the programme's web page before screening.
response.limitations: Rapid methods may miss studies; English-language restriction; indirect comparisons between strategies.
response.summary: No participant risk; equity considerations for older patients and patients with limited English; protocol posted before screening.

response.partnershipPlan: Two patient partners from the regional patient council review the plain-language summary for the committee; a surgeon, an anaesthetist and a clinic nurse review the strategy categories.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; comments to the regional patient advice service about cancelled or delayed surgery are summarised for context.

path.problem.rawNeed:
I lead the perioperative value programme for a regional health authority with eight hospitals. Surgeons and anaesthetists still order routine preoperative tests for healthy adults having low-risk ambulatory surgery: electrocardiograms, chest radiographs, full blood counts and coagulation studies, although our regional guidance has said for three years that they are not needed. A snapshot of 1,200 cataract, hernia and arthroscopy patients last spring found that 61 percent had at least one test the guidance advises against. The executive committee has asked which strategies actually reduce this kind of low-value testing, and whether stopping tests leads to more cancellations on the day of surgery or to harm.

We want to do a rapid review of strategies for reducing low-value preoperative testing in adults having low-risk ambulatory or elective surgery: feedback to clinicians on their own ordering, changes to order sets and electronic defaults, triage in the pre-anaesthesia clinic, clinician education, and materials for patients. We need to know which strategies, alone or combined, reduced testing, by how much, how long the effect lasted, and whether same-day cancellations or perioperative complications changed. The committee meets in December, so we have ten weeks.

I need help with a focused question, the outcomes, a search and screening approach that is quick without being careless, and a way to report certainty that the committee will understand. A librarian and two analysts are available part time.
path.problem.constraints: Ten weeks until the executive committee meeting in December. A librarian two days a week and two analysts one day a week each. English-language reports only. No budget for full-text purchase beyond the library's subscriptions.
